content: Other pathogens are contributing to the outbreak. Epidemiological investigations of outbreaks can provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of vaccines and the epidemiology of pertussis. This includes data on the distribution of cases and the case fatality ratio across different age groups. Interpreting an outbreak: An outbreak with high severity among infants may indicate gaps in immunization coverage. Conversely, an outbreak in older age groups could suggest changes in epidemiology, such as waning immunity, or alterations in surveillance practices. Modifications needed in surveillance: In countries using event-based or aggregate surveillance, once a cluster of cases is identified, a case investigation form should be used to investigate individual cases. Sporadic cases are not typically investigated or laboratory-confirmed in aggregate surveillance systems. For small outbreaks, surveillance should transition to line-listing individual cases. In larger outbreaks, data collection on a subset of cases can help understand the evolving epidemiology. For example, the first 5–10 cases should be confirmed to establish the outbreak, after which epidemiological linking can be used to conserve resources. After two or three incubation periods (approximately 1–2 months), the process may need to be repeated to confirm whether the pertussis outbreak is ongoing. For countries conducting case-based surveillance in sentinel sites: Surveillance can be expanded to include more reporting sites or a broader age range to better understand the outbreak's epidemiology. Consistency is essential for monitoring trends across sentinel sites over time. Countries may rely more on epidemiological linking of cases to reduce the burden on laboratories. Data management and reporting requirements: All reporting sites should immediately notify health authorities of suspected pertussis cases using any available communication method. The minimum information required includes patient identifiers and contact details. A mechanism should be established for weekly reporting to health authorities, including basic information on pertussis cases. If no cases are observed in a week, a zero report must still be submitted to confirm the surveillance system is operational. Each suspected case should be assigned a unique identification number (UID) that includes geographical location, year, and serial number. All communications and forms related to the case should reference this UID. Recommended data elements for case investigation include demographic information, clinical details, hospitalization status, treatment type, laboratory results, vaccination status, and epidemiological data. Data analysis should focus on time, place, and person characteristics to detect trends, clusters, or high-risk areas. Public health response: During an outbreak, vaccination efforts should prioritize unvaccinated or under-immunized individuals while strengthening routine immunization in the affected area. Vaccination campaigns are not typically part of the pertussis outbreak response. However, widespread use of PEP has not been shown to effectively control community-wide outbreaks. PEP may be appropriate in limited, closed settings with small numbers of cases and no ongoing community transmission. Multiple rounds of antibiotics are not recommended for continued transmission. Active case search and contact tracing should focus on symptomatic individuals in settings like schools, daycare centers, and hospitals. Early treatment of infants under six months with respiratory illness is critical. All public and private health facilities in affected and surrounding areas should be notified and encouraged to maintain a high index of suspicion for pertussis cases. Health promotion activities and educational materials should be distributed to raise awareness about pertussis and its prevention, particularly vaccination. Disease epidemiology: Pertussis, or whooping cough, is an acute bacterial respiratory disease caused by Bordetella pertussis. It is common among children worldwide but can also affect adolescents and adults. The disease is characterized by paroxysms of violent coughing, often followed by a high-pitched inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting. Infants under six months may not exhibit typical symptoms. Complications include pneumonia, seizures, encephalopathy, and, in rare cases, death, particularly among unvaccinated infants. Vaccines: Two types of pertussis vaccines are available: whole-cell vaccines (wP) and acellular vaccines (aP). Whole-cell vaccines are widely used in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) but may cause rare side effects. Acellular vaccines have fewer side effects but are less effective than whole-cell vaccines. High-income countries (HICs) have largely replaced whole-cell vaccines with acellular formulations. However, a resurgence of pertussis cases has been observed in some countries using acellular vaccines, potentially due to reduced vaccine efficacy and bacterial evolution. WHO recommends three doses of pertussis vaccine for all infants and one booster dose for children aged 1–6 years. Surveillance and specimen collection: Surveillance for pertussis is essential to monitor its epidemiology and control. Specimen collection methods include nasopharyngeal swabs, nasopharyngeal aspirates, and serum samples. Culture remains the most specific diagnostic test, but polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and serological testing are also valuable tools.
